890.title: Borobudur built
890.hook: in Java, a stone mountain of a monument, carved with the life and the Jataka
890.howItsDone: Buddhist pilgrims, especially at the Vesak festival, walk Borobudur's terraces clockwise, keeping the monument on their right, and the carved panels of the Buddha's life and past lives are read in order as they go.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pindapata, rice placed in silence in each bowl. Your line: the line at dawn.

From a distance, across the green fields of central Java, in Indonesia, it looks like a hill that someone has tidied. Gray stone stacked in terraces, narrowing as it rises, with a crown of bell-shaped stupas on top and volcanoes behind it. Walk closer and the stone turns into pictures. Panel after panel, wall after wall: a prince in a palace, a woman asleep, a forest hermit, a hare by a fire, ships at sea. There is no hall to step into out of the sun. The whole thing is meant to be walked.
screen: `A HILL OF TERRACES IN JAVA.` → `THE STONE TURNS INTO PICTURES.` → `NO HALL INSIDE. YOU WALK IT.`

segments.voice: First, the shape. Borobudur is a stupa, the same kind of monument as those at Sanchi and the Shwedagon. But its builders raised it over a natural hill, wrapping the hill in stone, terrace above terrace, so the stupa became a mountain you can climb. There is no room inside to gather in. The monument itself is the path. Second, the life of the Buddha in stone. Along the walls of one gallery, carved panels tell his story in order: the prince in the palace, the sights that troubled him, leaving home, the years of seeking, the awakening, the first teaching. Scholars match these panels to a Sanskrit telling of the life called the Lalitavistara. Third, the lives before that life. Other panels carve the Jataka, the stories of the Buddha's past births as an animal, a king, a merchant, a hermit. In one, a hare with nothing to offer a hungry traveler but himself leaps into the fire. Stories like these teach the long patience it takes to grow a bodhisattva's heart, one life at a time. Fourth, a book you read with your feet. The panels run in order around each terrace, so a pilgrim reads them by walking around the monument with it on the right, the way stupas are circled in respect, and climbs a terrace only after finishing the story below. Nobody hurries Borobudur. You read it slowly or not at all. Tomorrow, the climb itself, all the way to the top.
screen: `A STUPA BUILT OVER A HILL.` · `THE BUDDHA'S LIFE, PANEL BY PANEL.` · `THE JATAKA: LIVES BEFORE THAT LIFE.` · `A BOOK YOU READ WITH YOUR FEET.` · then, large: `A MOUNTAIN OF STONE.`

segments.voice: Stand in your mind at the foot of Borobudur in the early light, gray stone rising in steps above you, and let your eyes travel up, terrace by terrace, to the stupas on top. Then come back down to a single carved panel at eye level and look at it the way you'd look at a picture in a children's book, one figure, one gesture, one moment, breathing.
Borobudur built. A stupa raised over a hill in Java, terrace on terrace, carved with the Buddha's life and his past lives, meant to be read by walking. Today's word.
Your line: a mountain of stone. Every terrace holds a chapter of the story. That's day eight hundred ninety.

891.title: Walking Borobudur
891.hook: pilgrims climb from carvings of desire to open terraces and a plain stupa at the top
891.howItsDone: Pilgrims walk Borobudur from the bottom up, circling each level clockwise before climbing to the next, and at the Vesak festival monks and lay Buddhists process there with candles and chanting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Borobudur built, a stupa raised over a hill and carved with stories. Your line: a mountain of stone.

The first gallery of Borobudur is a narrow corridor, and the world shrinks. High stone walls rise on both sides: on your right, the carved panels of the main wall; on your left, the balustrade, carved too. Overhead, only a strip of sky. You walk, and read, and turn the corner, and walk again. Princes, palaces, hermits, animals, crowds. Then a stairway, and another gallery just like it, and another. Hours can pass in here. Then, near the top, you climb one more flight, and the walls are simply gone. Wind. Light. Open terraces, round instead of square, and the volcano on the horizon.
screen: `A NARROW GALLERY, WALLS OF STORIES.` → `A STRIP OF SKY OVERHEAD.` → `THEN THE WALLS ARE GONE.`

segments.voice: First, the bottom. At the very base of Borobudur is a hidden foot, a ring of carvings later covered over with stone. They show deeds and their results: people quarreling, hunting, gossiping, giving alms, and what each brings in its turn. Daily life, wanting and its fruit, is where the climb starts. Second, the galleries. Above that come the square, walled corridors: the Buddha's life, his past lives, and the long journey of a young seeker named Sudhana, who goes from teacher to teacher looking for the way. You can't see out. All you can see is story. Third, the open terraces. Then the walls end. The top levels are round and plain, with no carved scenes at all. Rows of stupas stand there, each one a stone lattice, like a bell made of open diamonds, and inside each sits a Buddha you can just glimpse through the gaps. Fourth, the top. In the middle stands one large, plain stupa, closed, and around it is nothing but sky. One reading, offered by scholars and guides, sees three Buddhist realms in the climb: the realm of desire at the base, the realm of form in the carved galleries, and the formless realm on the open terraces. Whether or not the builders drew it that neatly, the change is there in the walking: crowded pictures, then fewer, then none at all. The stories carry you up, and then they let you go.
screen: `AT THE BASE: DEEDS AND THEIR RESULTS.` · `WALLED GALLERIES OF STORY.` · `OPEN TERRACES, BUDDHAS IN LATTICE.` · `AT THE TOP: ONE PLAIN STUPA AND SKY.` · then, large: `FROM CARVINGS TO OPEN SKY.`

segments.voice: If there are stairs near you, climb them slowly, and if not, a single step, a doorway or your imagination will do, letting the weight come onto each foot before the next. Let your thoughts be as busy as the carved walls on the way up, let them thin out near the top, and at the last step stop, with just air and breath.

892.title: Vietnam
892.hook: where Theravada and Mahayana meet, and Chan becomes Thien
892.howItsDone: In Vietnamese pagodas, monks, nuns and lay Buddhists practice Thien meditation and also chant the name of Amitabha Buddha, while Khmer Theravada temples in the south keep Pali chanting and the morning alms.

segments.voice: Yesterday: walking Borobudur, up through walls of story to the open terraces. Your line: from carvings to open sky.

Two temples, one country. In the Mekong Delta, in the far south of Vietnam, monks in saffron robes chant in Pali under steep, gilded Khmer roofs. A long way north, in a pagoda near Hanoi, a nun in brown robes sits in silent meditation, and an hour later the same hall fills with lay people chanting the name of Amitabha Buddha, a Mahayana practice. Different robes, different languages, different streams of the teaching. Across Southeast Asia, both streams have shown up in stone: Theravada in Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand, Mahayana at Angkor and Borobudur. In Vietnam, they live side by side today.
screen: `SAFFRON ROBES IN THE MEKONG DELTA.` → `BROWN ROBES NEAR HANOI.` → `ONE COUNTRY, TWO STREAMS.`

segments.voice: First, the two streams. Mahayana Buddhism came into Vietnam with texts written in Chinese characters, and it shaped pagodas and monasteries across the country. Theravada lives on too, especially among the Khmer communities of the south, with Pali chanting and saffron robes, and some Vietnamese monasteries follow it as well. Second, Chan becomes Thien. One Mahayana school, called Chan in China and Zen in Japan, is called Thien in Vietnam. Its heart is meditation: sitting, seeing clearly, not relying on words alone. Tradition says all three names come from the old Indian word for meditation, dhyana. Third, a king on a mountain. Vietnamese tradition remembers a king named Tran Nhan Tong, who gave up his throne, became a monk, and went to live on Yen Tu mountain. The Thien school linked to him is called Truc Lam, the Bamboo Grove, and it's still practiced today. Fourth, both in one hall. In Vietnamese pagodas, Thien meditation and Pure Land chanting live side by side, sometimes on the same day, with the same people, who don't treat it as a choice they must make. And beneath both streams is shared ground. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in one line: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." A Khmer monk in the delta and a Thien nun near Hanoi could both say that line and mean it.
screen: `MAHAYANA AND THERAVADA, BOTH AT HOME.` · `CHAN IN CHINA, THIEN IN VIETNAM.` · `A KING WHO BECAME A MONK.` · `MEDITATION AND CHANTING, ONE HALL.` · then, large: `TWO STREAMS MEET.`

segments.voice: Think of a place in your own life where two ways live together, two languages in one kitchen, two family traditions at one holiday table, a morning person and a night owl under one roof. Notice where the two rub against each other and where they've quietly made room, and let both be there, side by side, without judging which is right.

893.title: Lumbini found
893.hook: Ashoka's pillar was found at Lumbini, marking the birthplace
893.howItsDone: Buddhists from different countries travel to Lumbini in Nepal as pilgrims, visiting the garden, the pool, the temple at the birth site and Ashoka's pillar, and some walk on to the other places named in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vietnam, where Mahayana and Theravada share one country. Your line: two streams meet.

A dig on the flat, hot plain of southern Nepal, close to the Indian border. Workers clear away earth around a stone column standing half buried near a small shrine. The pillar is broken at the top, and it's plain, no statue, no carving to speak of. But low on the shaft there's writing, in an old script. Someone copies the letters out, line by line. And the inscription turns out to say, more or less: this is the place. Here the Buddha was born.
screen: `A HALF-BURIED PILLAR IN NEPAL.` → `WRITING LOW ON THE SHAFT.` → `HERE THE BUDDHA WAS BORN.`

segments.voice: First, a place the texts remember. In the Sutta Nipata, a sage named Asita hears that a child has been born who will one day awaken, born in a village of the Sakyans, in the Lumbini country. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Buddha himself names the place of his birth as one of the places a faithful follower might visit and be moved. So the name was never lost from the scriptures. Second, a place that slipped out of sight. As Buddhism faded in India, the garden itself was overgrown, and where exactly it lay became a question rather than a fact. Third, a king's stone answers it. The pillar that came out of the ground was set up by Ashoka, the emperor met earlier this year. His inscription says, in plain words, that twenty years after he was anointed, the king came here himself and worshiped, because here the Buddha, the sage of the Sakyas, was born. He had a stone pillar raised, and he made the village of Lumbini free of tax, paying only an eighth share of its harvest. Fourth, why this matters. A holy place can rest on memory alone. This one also has a king's own words, carved at the spot. Pilgrims had a name; now they had a place to stand. Today Lumbini has gardens, a pool, temples built by Buddhists from different countries, and the old pillar, still standing, still saying the same thing. A sentence in stone, waiting in the ground until someone could read it.
screen: `THE TEXTS REMEMBER LUMBINI.` · `THE GARDEN SLIPS OUT OF SIGHT.` · `ASHOKA'S PILLAR: HERE HE WAS BORN.` · `A NAME BECOMES A PLACE TO STAND.` · then, large: `THE BIRTHPLACE FOUND.`

segments.voice: If you have a map nearby, find Lumbini in southern Nepal, just north of the border with India, or simply picture the flat green plain, the pool, the old pillar in the sun. Then sit with one thought for the rest of the time: the stupas, the chronicles and the golden towers of these weeks all began with a child born here.

894.title: Bodh Gaya restored
894.hook: the temple at the place of awakening, restored and visited again
894.howItsDone: Buddhist pilgrims come to the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya to sit, chant, make offerings and walk clockwise around the temple and the bodhi tree, and some do long sets of prostrations there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lumbini found, a king's pillar saying, here the Buddha was born. Your line: the birthplace found.

Late afternoon in Bodh Gaya, in the state of Bihar in India. A tall, tapering temple tower rises over the town, and behind it, a wide, old tree with heart-shaped leaves. Under the tree, prayer flags. On the stone railings, rows of butter lamps. Monks in maroon from the Himalayas sit beside monks in saffron from Thailand and nuns in gray from Korea. Someone is chanting in Pali, someone in Tibetan, someone silently doing prostrations on a wooden board, again and again. A leaf falls, and three people move to pick it up. It wasn't always like this here.
screen: `A TALL TOWER AND AN OLD TREE.` → `ROBES OF EVERY COLOR, ONE TREE.` → `IT WASN'T ALWAYS LIKE THIS.`

segments.voice: First, the tree. The Vinaya's own account of the awakening begins here: at Uruvela, on the bank of the Neranjara river, the newly awakened Buddha sits at the foot of the bodhi tree for seven days, taking in the joy of freedom. Bodhi means awakening, and the tree is named for what happened under it. Second, the seat. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha looks back on his striving and recalls his resolve: let only skin, sinews and bones remain, let flesh and blood dry up, he would not slacken his effort until he reached what effort could reach. Tradition places that resolve here, under the tree. Pilgrims came. A great temple rose beside the tree, and a stone slab, the vajrasana, the diamond seat, marks where tradition says he sat. Third, the long quiet. As Buddhism faded in India, the pilgrims thinned and the temple fell into neglect. Fourth, the return. Restorers came, among them workers sent from Burma and, later, British archaeologists, who rebuilt and repaired the temple. And tradition says the tree that grows there now descends from the very tree the Buddha sat under. Remember the cutting carried to Sri Lanka, the one tradition says still grows at Anuradhapura? Some accounts say the line came back the other way too, from that tree to this one. So Buddhists of different schools, from different lands, sit under the same branches. Nobody owns the moment of awakening. The tree just keeps growing, and people keep coming back to it.

895.title: Pressure and revival
895.hook: in the colonial era, monasteries lost their patrons, and lay and monastic revivals followed
895.howItsDone: Buddhist societies, Sunday schools and lay meditation centers that grew out of this era still run in Sri Lanka and Myanmar, where lay people study the teachings and practice meditation alongside monks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bodhi, and Bodh Gaya restored. Your line: back to the tree.

For a long time in Sri Lanka and Burma, the arrangement was simple. The king protected the monks, gave land to the monasteries, settled their disputes, and paid for their temples. The monks taught, kept the texts, and blessed the kingdom. Then European empires arrived. In Sri Lanka the British took the last kingdom. In Burma the last king was sent away into exile. The thrones that had held up the monasteries were simply gone, and new mission schools, run by Christian missionaries, became a road to a good job. So who feeds a monastery whose patron is gone?
screen: `THE KING PROTECTED THE MONKS.` → `THEN THE THRONES WERE GONE.` → `WHO KEEPS THE MONASTERY GOING?`

segments.voice: First, the loss. Without kings, monasteries lost their main patrons, and the old schools in the temples lost ground to new ones run by missionaries and colonial governments. For a while it looked, to some observers, as if the teaching might simply thin out. Second, monks turned outward. In Sri Lanka, monks began to speak up in public: they set up printing presses, published pamphlets in the local language, and took part in open debates with Christian missionaries before crowds. The teaching that had lived behind monastery walls came out into the town square. Third, lay people took the texts into their own hands. Buddhist societies formed, raised money, and opened Buddhist schools. In Burma, a monk named Ledi Sayadaw wrote plain manuals and taught meditation and the deeper teachings to ordinary lay people, not only to monks. Teachers who came after him carried that lay meditation far beyond Burma. Fourth, a line that suddenly fit. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "You yourself must make an effort. The Tathâgatas (Buddhas) are only preachers." With the kings gone, no throne was coming to hold the teaching up, so monks and lay people held it up themselves. There were hard sides to this era too: real losses, and some revivals that grew sharp and political. But what grew out of it, Buddhist schools, lay meditation, the teaching in plain language, is still around today. Pressure, it turned out, didn't only break things. It also woke people up.

896.hook: the Sri Lankan layman who campaigned to restore Bodh Gaya and spoke in Chicago
896.howItsDone: Dharmapala is remembered in Sri Lanka and India as a Buddhist reformer, and the society he founded still works for Buddhist sites and pilgrims, while the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya is cared for by a committee of Hindus and Buddhists.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ledi Sayadaw, and revival. This week: a mountain of stone, the climb to open sky, two streams in Vietnam, the birthplace found, and back to the tree. Your line: revival.

A young man from Colombo, dressed in white, comes to Bodh Gaya on pilgrimage. He has read about this place: the tree, the seat of awakening. What he finds is a temple in poor repair, in the hands of others, with few Buddhists to be seen. By his own account, he sits near the tree and makes up his mind: he will give his life to bringing Buddhists back to this place. He has no title. He isn't a monk. He isn't a king. What he has is a voice, and he decides to use it.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN IN WHITE AT BODH GAYA.` → `A TEMPLE IN POOR REPAIR.` → `HE DECIDES TO USE HIS VOICE.`

segments.voice: First, the name and the white cloth. He was born into a Sri Lankan family and took the name Dharmapala, protector of the Dharma, along with the title Anagarika, one who has left home. He lived without marrying and gave himself to the teaching, but through his campaigning years he stayed a layman; he was ordained a monk only near the end of his life. Second, Bodh Gaya. The temple and its lands had long been held by a Hindu monastery, under its head, the mahant. Dharmapala wanted Buddhists to have a say at the place of awakening. He founded a society to work for it, wrote, petitioned, raised money, and went to court. He did not win in his lifetime. After his death, the law set up a committee of Hindus and Buddhists to care for the temple together. Both sides held the place dear, and the answer, in the end, was to share it. Third, Chicago. At a great gathering of the world's religions held there, he stood up and spoke for Buddhism to an American audience. Fourth, the whole man. His life wasn't simple. Some of his writing was hard, even harsh, toward other communities, and historians still argue over that part of his legacy. He's remembered with admiration and with argument, both. But the thread through all of it is clear: he loved something, and he wouldn't keep quiet about it.
